question: What is a JWT and what is it made of?
title: JWT Structure Explained – Java Backend Security Interview
direct_answer: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, URL-safe token used for securely transmitting information between parties. It consists of three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots: Header.Payload.Signature. The header specifies the algorithm (like HS256), the payload contains claims (user data, expiry), and the signature verifies integrity using a secret key.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JWT structure and its role in stateless authentication
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the payload is encrypted — it's only base64-encoded and readable by anyone who decodes it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Proactively clarify that JWT provides integrity through the signature, not confidentiality — never put passwords or sensitive secrets in the payload

sections.title: JWT: A Self-Contained Token for Stateless Authentication
sections.content:
A **JWT (JSON Web Token)** is a compact, self-contained token that carries information about a user without requiring server-side session storage.

Think of it like a sealed envelope with a letter inside — anyone can see the letter if they unseal it, but the wax seal proves it hasn't been tampered with. JWTs solve the scalability problem of traditional sessions: instead of the server storing session data in memory or a database, the token itself contains all the necessary user information. The server just verifies the signature to trust the token. This makes JWTs ideal for **stateless REST APIs** where you want to authenticate users across multiple server instances without shared session storage. The token is **Base64URL-encoded**, making it safe to pass in HTTP headers or URLs. Each part (header, payload, signature) serves a distinct purpose: the header declares the signing algorithm, the payload holds the actual data (called **claims**), and the signature ensures no one has modified the token.

sections.title: The Three Parts of a JWT at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Header|~first segment, declares signing|alg names the algorithm (HS256/RS256)|typ is usually JWT|Base64URL-encoded, readable
emerald|Payload|~middle segment, carries claims|sub, iat, exp standard claims|custom claims like roles allowed|Base64URL-encoded, NOT encrypted
rose|Signature|~last segment, proves integrity|HMAC/RSA over header + payload|created with the secret key|tampering breaks verification

sections.title: Creating and Validating a JWT in Spring Boot
When to Use JWT
sections.content:
Use JWTs when you need **stateless authentication** across multiple servers or microservices — for example, a Spring Boot API deployed on three EC2 instances behind a load balancer, where any instance should authenticate a user without calling a shared session database.

Use them for **mobile app backends** where session cookies don't work well and you want the app to send the token in the Authorization header.

Use them in **single sign-on (SSO)** scenarios where a user logs in once and the token grants access to multiple services.

Avoid JWTs if you need frequent token revocation (like admin-triggered logout) — the stateless nature makes immediate revocation difficult unless you maintain a blacklist, which defeats the statelessness benefit.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating the payload as encrypted**: Freshers often think JWT hides the data because it looks encoded. The payload is only Base64URL-encoded — anyone can decode it and read the claims. Never put passwords, credit card numbers, or API keys in a JWT payload.
- **Not validating the signature**: Some implementations extract the payload without calling parseClaimsJws(), which skips signature verification. An attacker can then modify the token and the server will trust it. Always validate before using claims.
- **Using weak or hardcoded secrets**: Using "secret" or "12345" as the signing key makes JWTs trivially forgeable. In production, use a strong random key stored in environment variables, rotated regularly.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Three parts**: Header (algorithm metadata), Payload (claims like username and expiry), Signature (HMAC or RSA signature verifying integrity)
**Base64URL encoded**: Makes the token URL-safe and compact, but NOT encrypted — anyone can decode and read the payload
**Stateless**: Server doesn't store session data — all info is in the token itself, enabling horizontal scaling
**Signature purpose**: Proves the token wasn't tampered with — only someone with the secret key can create a valid signature
**Claims**: Standard claims include sub (subject/user), exp (expiration timestamp), iat (issued at) — custom claims can be added
**Algorithm choice**: HS256 (HMAC with SHA-256) uses a shared secret, RS256 (RSA) uses public/private key pairs for better security in distributed systems
**Expiration**: Always set an exp claim — tokens without expiry are security risks if leaked or stolen

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A JWT is a compact token that lets you authenticate users without storing session data on the server. It's made of three parts separated by dots: the header, the payload, and the signature. The header tells you what algorithm was used to sign it, like HS256. The payload is where you put the actual data, which we call claims — things like the username, when the token expires, and when it was issued. The signature is the security layer — it's created by taking the header and payload, signing them with a secret key, and that proves no one has tampered with the token. Here's the critical part freshers miss: the payload is only base64-encoded, not encrypted. Anyone can decode it and read what's inside. The signature doesn't hide the data, it just verifies integrity. So never put passwords or sensitive secrets in a JWT payload. In Spring Boot, you'd use a library like jjwt to create the token after a user logs in. You call Jwts.builder, set the subject to the username, add an expiration time, sign it with your secret key, and compact it into the final token string. When a request comes in with that token, you parse it with the same secret key — if the signature is valid, you trust the claims inside. That's how JWT enables stateless authentication: the token itself carries all the info you need, so your server doesn't have to look up sessions in a database.

beats.content: candidates miss: saying the JWT is 'encrypted' or 'secure' without qualification. The correct statement is: the signature verifies integrity, not confidentiality. The payload is readable by anyone.

question: How does JWT-based authentication work in a Spring Boot REST API?
title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot REST API
direct_answer: JWT authentication in Spring Boot works through a login endpoint that validates credentials and returns a signed JWT. A custom filter (extending OncePerRequestFilter) intercepts every request, extracts the JWT from the Authorization header, validates the signature, and sets the authenticated user in SecurityContextHolder. The session management is configured as STATELESS so no session data is stored on the server.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical implementation knowledge of JWT in Spring Security, not just theoretical understanding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing JWT in isolation without mentioning the filter chain, SecurityContext, or STATELESS session policy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the key components by role: JwtUtil for token operations, JwtAuthenticationFilter extending OncePerRequestFilter, SecurityConfig setting sessionCreationPolicy to STATELESS

sections.title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot REST API
sections.content:
JWT authentication in Spring Boot replaces traditional session-based auth with a **stateless token flow**. When a user logs in via a POST to /auth/login with username and password, the **AuthController** validates credentials (usually via **UserDetailsService**), and if correct, generates a JWT using a utility class.

This token is returned to the client in the response body or as a header. On every subsequent request, the client sends this token in the **Authorization: Bearer <token>** header. A custom **filter** (extending **OncePerRequestFilter**) intercepts the request before it reaches your controllers, extracts the token, validates the signature, and if valid, loads the user details and sets the **Authentication** object in the **SecurityContextHolder**. This tells Spring Security who the user is for this request. Crucially, the **SecurityConfig** must set **sessionCreationPolicy** to **STATELESS**, which tells Spring to never create or use HTTP sessions — every request is authenticated independently via the JWT. This architecture scales horizontally because no session state is shared between server instances.

Authorization: Bearer token] --> B{JwtAuthenticationFilter
OncePerRequestFilter} B --> C[Strip 'Bearer '
extract token] C --> D{Signature valid
and not expired?} D -- No --> E[401 Unauthorized] D -- Yes --> F[Load UserDetails
set SecurityContextHolder] F --> G[Controller handles
authenticated request] ```

sections.title: JWT Authentication Filter in Spring Security
When to Use JWT Authentication
sections.content:
Use JWT-based auth for **RESTful APIs** consumed by mobile apps, SPAs (single-page applications), or third-party services where session cookies aren't practical.

Use it when you need to **scale horizontally** — multiple Spring Boot instances behind a load balancer, where session replication would be complex and slow.

Use it in **microservices architectures** where each service needs to validate user identity without calling a central auth server every time — the JWT carries the necessary claims.

Avoid JWT if your use case requires **frequent token revocation** (like a banking app where you need to instantly invalidate tokens if fraud is detected) — JWTs are hard to revoke because they're stateless. In those cases, consider using opaque tokens with server-side validation or a hybrid approach with a token blacklist.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting to set sessionCreationPolicy to STATELESS**: Freshers often leave the default session policy, so Spring creates HTTP sessions even though you're using JWT. This defeats the purpose and wastes memory. Always configure SecurityConfig with sessionManagement().sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS).
- **Not checking if Authentication is already set**: The filter runs on every request, and if you don't check SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() == null, you might reprocess the same token multiple times or override existing authentication. The null check prevents redundant work.
- **Validating the token after setting SecurityContext**: Some implementations extract the username, set authentication, then validate — by that point the request is already authenticated with potentially invalid data. Always validate the token signature BEFORE setting the Authentication object.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **OncePerRequestFilter**: Base class ensuring the filter executes exactly once per request — prevents duplicate token validation in forwarded requests
**Authorization header format**: Standard is 'Bearer <token>' — the filter strips 'Bearer ' prefix to extract the raw JWT
**SecurityContextHolder**: Thread-local storage where Spring Security keeps the current user's Authentication object — setting it authenticates the user for that request
**STATELESS session policy**: Tells Spring Security to never create HttpSession — every request is authenticated independently via the token
**UserDetailsService**: Loads user details (username, authorities) from your database — the filter calls this after extracting the username from JWT
**Filter chain order**: The JWT filter must run BEFORE UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter — configured in SecurityConfig with addFilterBefore()
**Login endpoint**: Separate from the filter — POST /auth/login validates credentials via AuthenticationManager and returns a new JWT if successful

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JWT authentication in Spring Boot has two main parts: the login flow and the request validation flow. When a user logs in, they send their username and password to a POST endpoint like slash auth slash login. The controller validates those credentials, usually by calling the AuthenticationManager. If the credentials are correct, a utility class called JwtUtil generates a new JWT with the username and expiration time, signs it with a secret key, and returns it to the client. That's the login part. Now on every subsequent request, the client includes that JWT in the Authorization header with the format Bearer space token. Here's where the custom filter comes in. You create a class that extends OncePerRequestFilter — this ensures it runs exactly once per request. The filter's doFilterInternal method extracts the token from the header, strips the Bearer prefix, and passes it to JwtUtil to validate the signature and extract the username. If the token is valid, the filter loads the user details from UserDetailsService, creates a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken, and sets it in the SecurityContextHolder. This tells Spring Security who the user is for this request. After that, the request proceeds to your controller. The key config piece is in SecurityConfig: you must set the session creation policy to STATELESS. This tells Spring to never create HTTP sessions because you're doing stateless authentication with JWT. You also add the JWT filter before the default authentication filter in the filter chain. That's the full flow: login generates the token, the filter validates it on every request, and SecurityContext holds the authenticated user.

beats.content: sharp edge: forgetting to set SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS and forgetting to disable CSRF. Without STATELESS, Spring creates a session anyway. Without disabling CSRF, form submissions break. These two lines must go in your SecurityConfig.

question: What are the security risks of using JWT and how do you mitigate them?
title: JWT Security Risks and Mitigations – Java Backend
direct_answer: JWT security risks include algorithm confusion attacks (accepting alg:none), secret key leakage, lack of built-in token revocation, exposing sensitive data in the readable payload, XSS attacks when stored in localStorage, and tokens with no expiry. Mitigations: enforce strong algorithms, rotate secrets regularly, use short expiry with refresh tokens, store only non-sensitive claims, prefer HttpOnly cookies, and implement a token blacklist for critical revocations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Security maturity beyond basic JWT usage — understanding where JWT can fail and how to defend against attacks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming JWT is secure by default without considering algorithm attacks, storage vulnerabilities, or revocation challenges
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the alg:none vulnerability explicitly — it's a JWT-specific attack where the server accepts unsigned tokens if you don't validate the algorithm

sections.title: JWT Security Vulnerabilities and Defense Strategies
sections.content:
While JWTs provide a convenient mechanism for stateless authentication, they introduce several security risks that freshers often overlook. The most critical vulnerability is **algorithm confusion**, where an attacker changes the header to alg:none (no signature) and the server accepts it if not properly configured.

Another major issue is **secret key leakage** — if your signing key is exposed (hardcoded in Git, logged, or insufficiently random), attackers can forge valid tokens for any user. JWTs are also **difficult to revoke** because they're stateless — if a token is stolen, it remains valid until expiry. The **payload is readable** by anyone who base64-decodes it, so sensitive data exposure is a risk. **Client-side storage** introduces vulnerabilities: localStorage is accessible to JavaScript (XSS attacks), and cookies without proper flags are vulnerable to CSRF. Finally, **missing expiration** or overly long expiry times mean stolen tokens have a long attack window. Understanding these risks and implementing mitigations is what separates security-aware developers from those who just follow tutorials.

sections.title: JWT Risks Mapped to Mitigations
sections.content:
rose|Algorithm confusion|~alg:none attack|attacker drops the signature|server trusts unsigned token|fix: enforce algorithm whitelist
amber|Secret key leakage|~forged tokens|hardcoded or committed keys|weak random secret|fix: env var, rotate, RS256
violet|No revocation|~stolen token stays valid|stateless by design|long expiry widens window|fix: short expiry + refresh + blacklist
cyan|Unsafe storage|~XSS token theft|localStorage readable by JS|payload only Base64 encoded|fix: HttpOnly + SameSite cookie

sections.title: Secure JWT Configuration in Spring Boot
When to Apply JWT Security Mitigations
sections.content:
Apply **algorithm enforcement and key rotation** in all production JWT implementations — these are non-negotiable baseline defenses.

Use **short-lived access tokens (15-30 minutes) with refresh tokens** when you need a balance between security and user experience — the user stays logged in, but stolen access tokens expire quickly. Implement a **token blacklist** when handling high-value operations like financial transactions, admin actions, or account deletion, where you need the ability to immediately invalidate a token despite JWT being stateless.

Use **HttpOnly cookies with SameSite** for web applications to prevent XSS token theft.

Apply **payload encryption** (using JWE instead of JWT) only when you must include sensitive data that can't be stored elsewhere — but prefer redesigning to avoid putting sensitive data in tokens at all. In microservices, consider **RS256 (RSA signatures)** instead of HS256 so public keys can be distributed without exposing signing ability.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not validating the algorithm in the header**: Freshers call parseClaimsJws() but don't realize some libraries accept alg:none if not explicitly blocked. Always use parserBuilder().setSigningKey() which enforces signature validation — never parse the token manually with string splitting.
- **Storing the secret key in application.properties committed to Git**: The signing key should be an environment variable or secret manager entry, never hardcoded or version-controlled. Use at minimum a 256-bit random key for HS256.
- **Setting expiration to days or weeks**: A 7-day token gives attackers a week-long attack window if stolen. Use 15-30 minute access tokens with a separate refresh token for longer sessions.
- **Implementing blacklist in application memory**: Using a simple HashSet means the blacklist is lost on server restart and isn't shared across instances. Use Redis or a database for distributed blacklist storage.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Algorithm confusion**: The alg:none attack lets attackers remove the signature — mitigate by using parserBuilder with explicit key validation, never accept unsigned tokens
**Secret key security**: Use strong random keys (minimum 256 bits for HS256), store in environment variables, rotate regularly — leaked keys let attackers forge any token
**Token revocation challenge**: JWTs can't be invalidated server-side by design — implement a blacklist (Redis-backed) for critical revocations or use short expiry with refresh tokens
**Payload exposure**: Base64 encoding is not encryption — never put passwords, credit cards, or API keys in JWT payload, only non-sensitive identifiers
**XSS and localStorage**: Storing JWTs in localStorage exposes them to any XSS vulnerability — prefer HttpOnly cookies which JavaScript cannot access
**CSRF with cookies**: If using cookies for JWT storage, enable SameSite=Strict or Lax attribute, or implement CSRF token validation for state-changing operations
**Expiration best practice**: Access tokens should expire in 15-30 minutes — combine with refresh tokens (longer-lived, stored securely) for seamless user experience

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JWTs have several security risks you need to be aware of. The most critical is the algorithm confusion attack. If you don't validate the algorithm properly, an attacker can change the header to alg colon none, remove the signature, and your server might accept it as valid. The way you prevent this is by always using parserBuilder with setSigningKey — this enforces signature validation and rejects unsigned tokens. Never parse the token manually by splitting on dots. Another risk is secret key leakage. If your signing key is weak or gets exposed — like if you hardcode it or commit it to Git — attackers can generate valid tokens for any user. Always use a strong random key stored in environment variables and rotate it periodically. The third big issue is that JWTs are hard to revoke. Because they're stateless, there's no server-side session to kill. If a token is stolen, it's valid until it expires. The mitigation here is to use short expiration times, like fifteen or thirty minutes, combined with a refresh token for longer sessions. For critical operations like admin actions, you can maintain a token blacklist in Redis — it adds some state, but it's worth it for security. You also have to be careful about what you put in the payload. It's only base64-encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can decode it and read the claims. Never put passwords or credit card info in there. And finally, storage matters. If you store the JWT in localStorage, any XSS vulnerability lets an attacker steal it. The better approach is HttpOnly cookies with the SameSite attribute, which prevents JavaScript access and cross-site attacks.

beats.label: the risks
beats.content:
The main vulnerabilities:
- Algorithm confusion (alg:none): attacker sets the header algorithm to 'none' and the server skips signature verification — explicitly whitelist your expected algorithm
- Secret compromise: if the HS256 secret leaks, every token can be forged — use RS256 for high-value systems
- No revocation: a stolen token is valid until it expires — use short expiry (15-60 min) and refresh tokens
- Sensitive data in payload: the payload is Base64 encoded, not encrypted — visible to anyone
- localStorage storage: XSS can steal the token — use HttpOnly cookie instead

beats.label: the mitigations
beats.content: Use the jjwt library which enforces algorithm whitelisting. Set expiry (exp claim) on every token. Store tokens in HttpOnly cookies with SameSite=Strict. Pair short access tokens with longer-lived refresh tokens in your database for revocation capability.

beats.label: non-obvious
beats.content: non-obvious: the alg:none attack is specific to JWT and not widely known outside security circles. Mentioning it by name in an interview signals genuine security awareness, not just tutorial knowledge.

question: Where should you store a JWT on the client side?
title: Where to Store JWT on Client Side – Security Tradeoffs
direct_answer: The best place to store JWT on the client is in an HttpOnly cookie with SameSite=Strict attribute. This prevents XSS attacks (JavaScript can't access the cookie) and mitigates CSRF (SameSite blocks cross-site requests). LocalStorage and sessionStorage are vulnerable to XSS. Memory storage (JavaScript variable) is secure but lost on page refresh. Avoid localStorage despite its convenience.

interviewer_intent.testing: Security awareness of client-side storage options and their attack surface tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recommending localStorage because it's simple — interviewers watch for this as a red flag indicating lack of security awareness
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Articulate the full tradeoff: HttpOnly cookies sacrifice XSS exposure for CSRF risk, which we mitigate with SameSite or CSRF tokens — showing you understand the security reasoning

sections.title: Client-Side JWT Storage: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
Where you store a JWT on the client determines its attack surface.

The main threat models are **XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)**, where malicious JavaScript steals the token, and **CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)**, where an attacker tricks the browser into making authenticated requests. **LocalStorage** and **sessionStorage** are vulnerable to XSS — any JavaScript on the page can read them, including injected malicious scripts. **Memory storage** (just a JavaScript variable) is XSS-resistant because it's not accessible across page reloads, but it's lost when the user refreshes. **HttpOnly cookies** are the most secure because the browser automatically includes them in requests, but JavaScript cannot access them, blocking XSS attacks. However, cookies introduce **CSRF risk** — a malicious site can trigger requests to your API with the cookie attached. The mitigation is the **SameSite** attribute (Strict or Lax), which tells the browser to only send the cookie for same-site requests. The best practice is **HttpOnly cookie with SameSite=Strict** — it prevents both XSS and CSRF at the cost of slightly more complex backend configuration.

Storage Options at a Glance

rose|localStorage|~simplest, least safe|readable by any script|one XSS = stolen token|avoid in production
amber|sessionStorage|~cleared on tab close|still JS-readable|XSS risk remains|low-risk apps only

emerald|HttpOnly + SameSite cookie|~recommended default|JS cannot read it|SameSite blocks CSRF|best balance

sections.title: When to Use Each Storage Option
sections.content:
Use **HttpOnly cookie with SameSite=Strict** for production web applications where security is critical — this is the recommended default for SPAs and server-rendered apps.

Use **memory storage** during development or for high-security apps where you're okay with the user logging in again on every page refresh — some banking apps do this intentionally.

Use **sessionStorage** (with caution) if you need the token to survive refresh but want it cleared when the user closes the browser tab — still vulnerable to XSS, so only for lower-risk apps. **Avoid localStorage** in production unless you've done a thorough XSS risk assessment — it's the most dangerous option despite being the simplest. For mobile apps or Electron desktop apps, the threat model is different (no XSS/CSRF), so secure platform storage like iOS Keychain or Android Keystore is preferred. Never use localStorage if your app has any user-generated content or third-party scripts.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Choosing localStorage for convenience**: Freshers often pick localStorage because tutorials show it and it's just two lines of code (localStorage.setItem, localStorage.getItem). Interviewers see this as a security red flag. Any XSS vulnerability — even from a third-party script or a comment section — can steal the token. Always articulate why you'd avoid it.
- **Not setting SameSite on cookies**: Setting a cookie without SameSite leaves it vulnerable to CSRF attacks where a malicious site triggers authenticated requests. Always specify SameSite=Strict or Lax. Strict is more secure (cookie only sent for same-site navigation), Lax allows some cross-site scenarios like following a link.
- **Assuming HttpOnly means the cookie can't be sent in requests**: HttpOnly means JavaScript can't read the cookie value, but the browser still automatically includes it in HTTP requests to the same domain — that's the whole point. This isn't a vulnerability, it's the intended behavior.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **XSS risk**: LocalStorage and sessionStorage are readable by any JavaScript — one XSS vulnerability and the token is stolen
**HttpOnly attribute**: Prevents JavaScript from accessing the cookie via document.cookie — blocks XSS-based token theft entirely
**SameSite attribute**: Tells browser to only send cookie for same-site requests — Strict blocks all cross-site, Lax allows safe navigation like GET from links
**CSRF vulnerability**: Cookies are automatically included in requests — without SameSite, a malicious site can make authenticated requests on behalf of the user
**Memory storage**: Storing token in JavaScript variable (not localStorage) is XSS-resistant but lost on page reload — used in very high-security apps
**Secure flag**: Always set Secure=true in production so the cookie is only sent over HTTPS — prevents man-in-the-middle attacks on unsecured networks
**Backend setup**: Using HttpOnly cookies requires CORS configuration (credentials: 'include' in fetch) and the backend must set the cookie in the login response with Set-Cookie header

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The best place to store a JWT is in an HttpOnly cookie with the SameSite attribute set to Strict. Here's why. LocalStorage is the most common choice because it's simple — you just call localStorage.setItem — but it's also the most dangerous. Any XSS vulnerability on your site, even from a third-party script or a compromised dependency, can read localStorage and steal the token. It's a one-line attack. SessionStorage has the same problem. It's slightly better because it's cleared when you close the tab, but it's still accessible to JavaScript, so XSS is a risk. Some people store the token in memory, just a JavaScript variable, which is secure against XSS because it's isolated to the runtime. But you lose it on page refresh, so the user has to log in again. That's actually intentional in some banking apps for extra security. Now, HttpOnly cookies solve the XSS problem completely. When you mark a cookie as HttpOnly, the browser blocks JavaScript from reading it via document.cookie. So even if an attacker injects a script, they can't steal the token. The cookie is still automatically included in requests to your API, which is what you want. But cookies introduce a different risk: CSRF, where a malicious site tricks your browser into making authenticated requests. The mitigation is the SameSite attribute. If you set SameSite equals Strict, the browser only sends the cookie for requests that originate from your own site. Cross-site requests won't include it. That blocks CSRF. So the combination of HttpOnly plus SameSite equals Strict gives you protection against both XSS and CSRF. The trade-off is your backend has to set the cookie in the login response using the Set-Cookie header, and your frontend needs to configure fetch with credentials colon include for CORS.

beats.label: storage comparison
beats.content:
| Storage | XSS risk | CSRF risk | Notes |
|---------|----------|-----------|-------|
| localStorage | High | None | Script-accessible, easily stolen |
| HttpOnly cookie | None | Medium | Mitigate CSRF with SameSite=Strict |
| In-memory (JS var) | Low | None | Lost on refresh, needs silent refresh |

beats.label: recommended pattern
beats.content: For production SPAs: store the short-lived access token in memory only. Store the refresh token in an HttpOnly SameSite=Strict cookie. On page load or 401 response, the client silently hits /auth/refresh to get a new access token using the cookie.

beats.label: production trap
beats.content: production trap: recommending localStorage because it's the default in every tutorial. Interviewers know this is the insecure path. State the XSS risk explicitly and recommend HttpOnly cookie instead.

question: How do you handle JWT expiry and token refresh?
title: JWT Expiry and Token Refresh – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: JWT expiry is handled with two token types: short-lived access tokens (15-60 minutes) for API requests, and long-lived refresh tokens (days to weeks) stored securely. When the access token expires, the client sends the refresh token to a /auth/refresh endpoint, receives a new access token, and retries the failed request. Refresh token rotation (invalidating the old refresh token on each use) prevents replay attacks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of production-grade token lifecycle management beyond basic JWT issuance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting long expiry on access tokens to avoid refresh complexity — defeats the security purpose of short-lived tokens
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the complete flow including refresh token rotation, where each refresh invalidates the previous refresh token to prevent reuse if stolen

sections.title: JWT Lifecycle Management with Access and Refresh Tokens
sections.content:
JWTs have an **expiration claim** (exp) that marks when they become invalid. If you set a long expiry (say 7 days) on access tokens, a stolen token remains usable for the full duration — that's a huge security risk.

The industry solution uses **dual-token architecture**: short-lived **access tokens** (15-60 minutes) authenticate each API request, while long-lived **refresh tokens** (7-30 days) are stored securely and used ONLY to obtain new access tokens. When an access token expires, the client doesn't re-prompt for username/password — it silently calls a refresh endpoint with the refresh token, gets a fresh access token, and continues. **Refresh token rotation** adds an extra layer: each time you use a refresh token, the server invalidates it and issues a new one. If an attacker steals an old refresh token, it's already burned. Think of access tokens as temporary passes to enter rooms, and the refresh token as your ID card to get new passes — you don't hand out your ID card with every door swipe.

sections.title: Access + Refresh Token Lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A[Login success] --> B[Issue access token 15m
+ refresh token 7d] B --> C[Call API with
access token] C --> D{Access token
expired?} D -- No --> C D -- Yes 401 --> E[POST /auth/refresh
with refresh token] E --> F{Refresh token
valid in DB?} F -- No --> G[Force re-login] F -- Yes --> H[Issue new access token
rotate refresh token] H --> C ```

sections.title: Spring Boot Token Refresh Flow with Rotation
When to Use This Dual-Token Pattern
sections.content:
Use this pattern in **production REST APIs** where users stay logged in for extended periods (web apps, mobile apps). If your app is a single-page application (SPA) where users work for hours, you can't keep popping login screens every 15 minutes. The refresh mechanism keeps sessions alive without storing passwords.

Use **refresh token rotation** in high-security contexts like banking or healthcare apps — each refresh burns the old token, so even if an attacker intercepts one, it's a one-time-use window. Skip this complexity for **internal tools** with 8-hour sessions or **short-lived dashboards** where users don't mind re-authenticating. For **server-to-server APIs** (microservices calling each other), client credentials flow with long-lived access tokens is simpler since there's no user session to maintain.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Setting 7-day expiry on access tokens**: Freshers avoid refresh logic by making access tokens live for days. This defeats the purpose — a stolen token is valid for a week. Access tokens should be short (15-60 min) so compromised tokens expire quickly.
- **Storing refresh tokens in localStorage**: Browser localStorage is vulnerable to XSS attacks. Store refresh tokens in httpOnly secure cookies or in-memory variables for SPAs. If using cookies, set SameSite=Strict to prevent CSRF.
- **Not invalidating refresh tokens on logout**: Freshers forget to delete refresh tokens from the database on logout. If a user logs out, their refresh token should be immediately revoked so no one can use it to mint new access tokens.
- **Allowing unlimited refresh token reuse**: Without rotation, a leaked refresh token can be used indefinitely until it expires. Each refresh should invalidate the old token and issue a new one.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Access token**: Short-lived JWT (15-60 min) sent with every API request in Authorization header, contains user claims
**Refresh token**: Long-lived opaque token (7-30 days) stored in database, used ONLY at /auth/refresh endpoint to get new access tokens
**Token rotation**: Each refresh operation invalidates the old refresh token and issues a new one, limiting damage from token theft
**Expiry claim (exp)**: Unix timestamp in JWT payload, checked by Spring Security filters to reject expired tokens automatically
**Client retry logic**: When API returns 401 Unauthorized, client calls /auth/refresh with refresh token, then retries original request with new access token
**Storage best practices**: Access tokens in memory or sessionStorage (short-lived, less risk), refresh tokens in httpOnly cookies (inaccessible to JavaScript)
**Revocation**: Store refresh tokens in database (unlike stateless access tokens) so you can delete them on logout or security events

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JWT expiry is handled with a two-token system. Access tokens are short-lived, typically fifteen to sixty minutes, and they're what you send with every API request. Refresh tokens are long-lived, maybe seven to thirty days, and they're stored securely on the backend. Here's how it works. When a user logs in, the server gives them both tokens. The client uses the access token for API calls. When that token expires, the API returns a four-oh-one error. The client then sends the refresh token to a dedicated endpoint, like slash-auth-slash-refresh. The server validates the refresh token, generates a new access token, and sends it back. The client retries the original request with the fresh token. The key security feature is rotation. Each time you use a refresh token, the server invalidates it and issues a new one. This means if an attacker steals an old refresh token, it's already burned and won't work. The common mistake freshers make is setting long expiry times on access tokens to avoid refresh complexity. That defeats the purpose because a stolen token stays valid for days. You want access tokens to expire quickly so the window of risk is small. In production, you'd also store refresh tokens in a database table so you can revoke them immediately if a user logs out or if you detect suspicious activity. This dual-token pattern is standard in production REST APIs and mobile apps where users stay logged in for extended periods.

speakable_v2.hook: Short-lived tokens expire and users shouldn't have to re-login. The refresh token pattern solves this cleanly.

beats.label: two token model
beats.content: At login, issue two tokens. The access token is short-lived (15-30 minutes) and used in the Authorization header for every API call. The refresh token is long-lived (7-30 days), stored in an HttpOnly cookie, and used only to obtain a new access token.

beats.label: refresh flow
beats.content: When the access token expires, the API returns 401. The client silently POSTs to /auth/refresh with the refresh token cookie. The server validates it exists in the database and hasn't expired, then issues a new access token and rotates the refresh token (old one is invalidated). If a rotated token is reused, it signals theft — invalidate all refresh tokens for that user.

beats.label: gotcha
beats.content: gotcha: setting access tokens to 7-day expiry 'to keep things simple.' That defeats the security benefit of short-lived tokens. The refresh complexity exists for a reason — stolen access tokens should expire quickly.
